newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lebanese on trial for fatal German hostel fire.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese on trial for fatal German hostel fire.

text.p: A young Lebanese refugee went on trial on Monday accused of starting a fire that killed 10 people last January in the worst disaster to hit an asylum-seekers' hostel in Germany.

Safwan Eid, a civil war refugee who had lived in the house in the northern city of Luebeck since 1990 with nine members of his family, was charged with aggravated arson and negligently causing bodily harm.
Prosecutors initially charged him with murder but later revised this.
The fire killed six people from Zaire, a man from Benin, a Lebanese and a woman from Angola with her six-year-old daughter. Thirty eight people were injured.
Prosecutors say Eid confessed to a first aid worker -- now the chief prosecution witness -- on the night of the blaze.
Eid's lawyer Gabriele Heinecke said he was too distraught to speak on the first day of his trial but would make a statement later. "The accused says he is innocent," she told the court on his behalf.

Eid could still face life imprisonment, if convicted, unless the court decides to treat him as a juvenile. Eid gave his age as 20, which means he could be treated as a juvenile at the court's discretion and face a maximum 10-year sentence.
But prosecutors say he was already 21 at the time the fire occurred. Eid's father Marwan told the court he had nine children and did not know the exact date of Safwan's birth.
Speaking in Arabic, he described how he was woken up on the night of January 18 as the iron gate to the hostel creaked open.
"Safwan and his two brothers were asleep in the attic at the time," he told the court. Marwan Eid said he heard a bang, looked out and saw the entrance of the hostel in flames.
Eid's defence team say the fire started on the ground floor near the entrance, suggesting an attack from outside. They will call a fire expert as witness who says he has evidence of this.
But prosecutors say Eid wanted revenge on a neighbour after a row, and started the blaze with petrol on a first-floor landing while residents including his family were asleep.
Eid's defence lawyer will also say prosecutors did not properly investigate four youths, including a skinhead from a local far-right group, who were detained near the scene.
Three of the young men, driving a stolen car, had singed hair. But police accepted their alibis and released them.

Most of the occupants of the hostel were asylum-seeking refugees from the Middle East and Africa along with ethnic German immigrants from Poland, fanning speculation that the fire had been a racist attack.
Anti-racist and left-wing groups demonstrated outside the court to lobby for Eid's release, saying he was a victim of racial persecution and that the fire was a neo-Nazi attack.
The blaze last January recalled an upsurge of neo-Nazi violence, including firebomb attacks on Turkish homes in Solingen and Moelln, following German unification in 1990.
